newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW-Unilever to look at part sale.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Unilever to look at part sale.

text.p: Anglo-Dutch consumer group Unilever Plc will consider offers for all or part of its four speciality chemicals divisions and hopes to conclude a sale in the next three to six months, chairman Niall FitzGerald told Reuters in an interview.
"We will now seek actively buyers for the totality or the individual businesses and we will then assess those over the next month or two," he said.
"We would hope to conclude a sale in the course of the next three to six months," he added.

FitzGerald declined to say how much the businesses might be worth. The four businesses -- National Starch and Chemical Company, Quest International, Unichema International and Crosfield -- have a combined turnover of 3.0 billion stg, and showed operating profit of 415 million in 1996, with margins of 14.1 percent.
The sale will enable Unilever to focus resources on its core consumer goods business, said FitzGerald.

"These are extremely large and important parts of our businesses but for some time we have been reviewing whether they should be a continuing part of the portfolio -- not because they are poorly performing themselves, they are excellent performers -- but whether we can give them the concentration and the focus that they require," said FitzGerald.
The four companies together make up one of the world's largest speciality chemicals groups, employing some 15,800 people in more than 35 countries.

"The whole speciality chemicals industry is in the process of fairly active realignment and we think that they are more likely to do better aligned with other businesses in the chemicals industry," said FitzGerald.
National Starch and Chemical Company based in the U.S. makes industrial adhesives, resins, speciality chemicals and starches.

Quest International produces food flavours and ingredients and Unichema International is a global leader in processing natural oils. Both are based in the Netherlands. Crosfield, based in Britain, makes surface coatings for products like toothpaste and food ingredients.
"They are essentially industrial businesses selling not to consumers but to intermediate customers. They are very fine busineses," FitzGerald said.

"But if you look at the way this industry is developing we have to take a decision either to significantly improve our presence in these markets, perhaps double it, or to exit and in exiting to concentrate on the other 90 percent of our business which is our mainstream consumer goods business."
FitzGerald added that the decision to sell was not an easy one especially given that the speciality chemicals division has peformed so well.

Earlier Unilever announced a 15 percent increase in annual profits before tax to 2.66 billion stg on a six percent rise in turnover. The result exceeded analysts' forecasts which centred on 2.525 billion for the year to December 31, 1996, up from 2.319 billion.
On the outlook FitzGerald said the overall economic situation in 1997 was likely to be generally favourable, as in 1996, but he warned on market conditions in Europe.
Unilever shares soared 90-1/2p in early trade to 1482-1/2p.
